title: Git for Scientists
text:
Lars Schöbitz





Data steward at Global Health Engineering, ETH Zurich
RStudio certified instructor since 2020
I teach people who have never written code or used Git


I finished these slides yesterday. That is on purpose, and at 11:10 I say why.



Block 09:30 to 09:40. Three facts, one sentence on the day before. No more here.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Two seats today
You sit on two seats at the same time.


Learner
09:40 to 10:30
Commit, branch and pull request: you make a commit of your own and watch a file travel into a shared repository.

Educator
10:40 to 11:30
You look at how this workshop is built and taught, and you give feedback on the first hour.


From now on, watch how I teach: what I say, how I say it, how I run the room. After the break you write it down.


Block 09:30 to 09:40. Say both seats out loud. The feedback after the break follows three words: content, presentation, interaction.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
One board for the room












https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVEMVk3OQ=/

No account, no name. Your notes are anonymous.
Parked questions: any time, one question per note.
One activity after the break.


An AI session (Claude) on my laptop reads the activity and groups your notes into one slide. Do not write names or anything personal on a note.



Block 09:30 to 09:40. Wait until the board is open on a few screens. Paper sticky notes are on the tables for whoever prefers them or if the board fails. Not every parked question gets an answer in two hours; the open ones get one by email.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Find your neighbour

Raise your hand if you use Git every week.
Now look around. If you have never used Git, sit beside a raised hand. Move now, with your laptop.


You work in pairs today, each person on their own laptop.
Pre-work not finished? Sit with a neighbour who has it and follow on their laptop.


 

Block 09:30 to 09:40. People who use Git weekly sit beside first-time users.

Your answers to the open question, grouped:


9

3

3
Git and AI tools



This is not a course about AI. What agents such as Claude Code do in a repository rests on the steps of today.
Things may go wrong here. Everything we do today can be undone.


Block 09:30 to 09:40, last slide of it. Groups only, no single answers: the survey promised that. Four answers fall outside these groups (collaboration in a team, repairing mistakes). Two anchor sentences out loud: not an AI course, everything can be undone.

title: Git for Scientists

How we work
Three ways of working. The one that applies is at the top of the slide.
My turn I show something on my screen. You watch and type nothing.
Our turn We do the same step at the same time: I on my screen, you on yours.
Your turn You work on a task, with your neighbour. I help where it sticks.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What is a commit?
A commit is a saved state of your files, with four pieces of information:

Who made it: a name and an email address
When: date and time
What changed: line by line
Why: the message you write with it


Block 09:40 to 09:50. Key words only, then the traces in a real repository on the next slide.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Traces in a real repository
My turn
The website of this workshop, public on GitHub: gitforsci-rdc/website

14 commits from 9 to 17 November
9 November: “pre-work site for the RDC 2026 iteration, steps 1 and 2 visible”
15 November, a Sunday, 22:00: “pre-work steps 3 to 5 for the GitHub Desktop route”
17 November: “pre-work step 6, your own repository and first commit”


A question for you: When were your instructions written?


9 of the 14 commits are from the last three days, 4 of them after 22:00.

Git forgets nothing. That is the use of it, and it is the reason to choose what goes into a commit.

Block 09:40 to 09:50. No browser needed, the slide carries it. The history shows that my instructions came late. This returns at 10:55.

One repository, several places





Pictures: Lars Schöbitz, CC BY 4.0


Block 09:40 to 09:50. Kim creates the repository on GitHub. Kim and Robin clone: three places, the same state. Laptops never talk to each other directly, always through GitHub. Words: local is the laptop, remote is GitHub. Clone once. A second clone is a second copy on the same laptop, and the two get mixed up.

title: Git for Scientists

Commits on GitHub
My turn
I show the repository teaching-rainbow-train in the browser.

From GitHub Desktop to GitHub: menu Repository, View on GitHub
The list of commits: the clock with the number
One commit up close: who, when, what, why
Verified beside a commit: it was made in the browser, and GitHub signed it. A commit from your laptop has no such mark. Both are fine.


Block 09:50 to 10:00. I show GitHub and explain, the room watches. Then the next slide: your turn, 3 minutes.

title: Git for Scientists

Your commits on GitHub
Your turn


In GitHub Desktop: menu Repository, View on GitHub. Your repository opens in the browser.
Click the clock with the number above the list of files on the right, for example 3 Commits.
Show your neighbour one commit: who, when, what, why.


The same commits as in GitHub Desktop. Your laptop and GitHub hold the same state.

 

Block 09:50 to 10:00. 3 minutes, each person on their own laptop. Without pre-work: look at the neighbour’s screen.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
A commit of your own
Our turn


In GitHub Desktop, choose your repository teaching-your-username. Menu Repository, Show in Finder (Windows: Show in Explorer).
Open the file your-username.md in a text editor and add one line at the end:
- What I want to take away today:
Write your answer behind it and save the file.
Back in GitHub Desktop: the tab Changes shows your line in green.
Write a message at the bottom left, for example Add what I want to take away, and click Commit to main.
Click Push origin.



Pushed? Thumbs up. Your repository on GitHub now shows one commit more.


Block 10:00 to 10:05. I do every step as rainbow-train at the same time, one step, then wait for the room. Push rejected: the commit carries the real email address, and the account blocks such pushes. In GitHub Desktop: Settings (Windows: File, Options), Git, tab Author, choose the address ending in users.noreply.github.com, Save. Then Undo at the bottom of Changes and commit again. Whoever is not ready follows on the neighbour’s laptop. This step returns at 11:25, done alone.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
A button is a command
My turn
GitHub Desktop runs commands for you. In a terminal, in RStudio, in Positron and in VS Code they carry these names:



In GitHub Desktop
The command




History
git log


Changes
git status


Commit to main
git commit


Push origin
git push


Fetch origin, Pull origin
git pull




What you learn today carries over to the tool you teach with.


Block 10:05 to 10:15, first slide of it. No live terminal. One sentence: an agent such as Claude Code works with the same commands.

title: Git for Scientists

text:
Create a branch, then open a pull request








K is Kim, R is Robin. Dashed: only on the laptop. Dark border: the newest commit of a branch.


Block 10:05 to 10:15, this slide and the next. Branch: a line of work of your own, main stays untouched. A commit, another commit, only then the push: solid, now also on GitHub. Pull request: the request to take the branch into main. In the picture it stands below the newest commit.

title: Git for Scientists
section: Robin works at the same time
text:
Robin works at the same time








The same steps for Robin, one after the other. Last picture: each person has a branch of their own, which is why yours is named people-username. GitHub holds everything, each laptop only its own work.

title: Git for Scientists
section: From your repository into the shared one
text:
From your repository into the shared one


Before

Your three lines are in your own repository teaching-your-username, in the file your-username.md
Only you write there


After

The same file is also in the shared repository workshop, in the folder people, on a branch of your own
A pull request asks to take it into main
A second person reads it, and merges it



You copy the file. Never the repository folder: it carries a hidden folder .git, and Git then sees a repository inside a repository.

title: Git for Scientists
section: A file goes into the shared repository
text:
A file goes into the shared repository
My turn

Lean back and watch. I work with the account rainbow-train, as a participant like you.


Open the repository workshop and click Fetch origin
Create the branch people-rainbow-train
Copy the file rainbow-train.md into the folder people
Commit
Publish the branch
Open the pull request and request a reviewer


Block 10:15 to 10:30. Two passes. First pass without stopping, about 4 minutes. Second pass slowly, and say these out loud before they meet them: 1. You cloned workshop in Step 5. Do not clone it again. Current Repository, workshop. 2. Current Branch, New Branch. The button at the bottom left must end in “to people-your-username”. If it ends in “to main”, you are on the wrong branch. 3. In Finder or Explorer: gitrepos/teaching-username, copy the one file, paste into gitrepos/workshop/people. The file, never the folder. 4. Changes shows one file with a tick. 5. Publish branch. 6. Preview Pull Request, then Create Pull Request at the bottom right. The browser opens. Fill in the two lines. On the right, Reviewers: the username of your neighbour. The room does not type here. Say it: this is your part at home, and the page has every step.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
A second person reads
My turn







Block 10:15 to 10:30, at about 10:25. Comment, commit, push, merge, one after the other, pictures only. No live review today.

What I showed is yours to do after the workshop, in about 30 minutes:


Open the page: gitforsci-rdc.github.io/website/workshop/add-your-file.html
Bring your file into the shared repository workshop with a pull request.
Request larnsce as the reviewer. I read every pull request that is open by Friday 4 December and write one question on it.



The second session of this course is where pairs review and merge each other’s work, 30 minutes of it. Today it is left out, and I say so because it is the part I would never cut from a full course.


Block 10:15 to 10:30, last slide before the break. The course is built in two sessions with time between them to practise. Today is the first session only.

text:
How this workshop is built
Everything you used this week is a repository.







What you saw
What it is




The website with the six steps
A repository, built into a site on every merge


The survey
A small app, its answers in a database

The comment after you ticked a box

A text file in the same repository as the website




One course organisation on GitHub for you, one for the material, one for the administration. The next cohort gets a new copy of the first one.


Block 10:55 to 11:00, this slide and the next, while the synthesis of activity 1 runs. One sentence per row. The point: the workshop teaches the tool it is built with, and every step you took left a trace I could see without asking.

title: Git for Scientists

What you wrote
Your notes from activity 1, grouped. I switch to the second tab.

Read it with your neighbour: which point surprises you? Then the floor is open, for what you wrote and for your questions.


Block 11:00 to 11:10. Switch to the browser tab with live.html. Give the room a minute to read. Read one positive and one negative theme per row out loud, then open it: who wants to say more on a negative one? Questions from the frame Parked questions fit here too. If the synthesis failed: open the board itself and read three notes per cell. Do not defend, say thank you and name one thing I will change.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Words I leave out
just   easily   quickly

They say that a step costs nothing. A learner who is stuck on it hears: it is me.
This morning: look for one of them on my slides or in the six steps of the pre-work. Found one? Park it on the board.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. If someone finds one, thank them and fix it in a commit after the workshop.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Design for the novice

Assume that people know nothing about the tool.
No gap between two steps: every click is written down.
Extra material for people with experience, marked as extra.


This morning: six pre-work steps with every click. “A button is a command” was the extra for those who use a terminal.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. The pre-work is where the novice design lives: a first-time user went from no account to a pushed commit in about an hour.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Know the learners, then design

A survey before anything is written: 27 answers decided the software and the pairs.
A tracker shows who is where in the pre-work, without asking anyone.
The content of today was written yesterday. Most learners do the pre-work on the last day, and I teach better from what I read then than from a plan made weeks ago.


It takes practice, and trust in the method, to walk into a room with slides that are one day old.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. This is the answer promised at 09:30. The method is fixed (My turn, Our turn, Your turn, pairs, a learner account), the content moves with the group. Next slide: one choice the survey led to.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Why GitHub Desktop?
Your preference in the survey:


11
RStudio


6
GitHub Desktop


4
Positron


5
no preference


I chose against the largest group. Half of the room does not write code in R, and 10 of you do not use Git today. GitHub Desktop needs no programming language, and its buttons carry the names of the commands.

Not shown on 20 November, for reading. The honest version: the choice has a cost for the 11.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
A learner account

Every demo this morning ran as rainbow-train: a second account with the rights you have, on the screens you see.
With my own account I am an owner. Buttons differ, warnings never show.
The account found the rejected push with the real email address before you did.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Costs one free account and one more browser profile.

title: Git for Scientists
section: Type with the room, mistakes included
text:
Type with the room, mistakes included

Participatory live coding: I type, you type, nothing is pasted.
A demo in two passes: once without stopping, once slowly.
A mistake on my screen is a moment to take apart together.


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. Then the next slide: the mistakes of Tuesday, and what they changed for today.

title: Git for Scientists
section: The same design, three days ago
text:
The same design, three days ago
On Tuesday I ran this design in German, online, for 16 people who do not write code.

13 pull requests in two hours, from people who had never used Git
Three clones of one repository on one laptop: “clone once” is now a sentence in your Step 6
A copied repository folder, with its hidden .git: today you copied one file
The real email address in most first commits, although the account said private: the setting in GitHub Desktop comes first
Too many emails before the workshop


Not shown on 20 November, for reading. The second cohort stays unnamed. Each line is a change you met this week: the instructions you followed are three days old.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What motivates adults to learn





Self-efficacy: I am in control of my own life.
Utility: This will help me meet my goals.
Community: People I know are learning this with me.


This morning: a repository of your own, your own three lines, a neighbour.



Figure and wording: Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, slides on motivation, CC BY 4.0. Art from openclipart.org.


Block 11:15 to 11:20, this slide and the next. Motivation is the strongest predictor of whether an adult learns something.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What takes motivation away



Unpredictability: What I do does not seem to affect the outcome.
Unfairness: The teacher plays favourites.
Indifference: Nobody cares.


A push that is rejected without a reason I can read is unpredictability. An instructor who answers only the fast people is unfairness.





For your own teaching: which of the three do your learners meet most often?


Figure and wording: Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, slides on motivation, CC BY 4.0. Art from openclipart.org.


Block 11:15 to 11:20. Ask for one hand per heading. One moment of my own if there is room: a course where the setup failed and the instructor went on.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Activity 2: what demotivated you
Your turn

On the board, frame Activity 2. 5 minutes, on your own.
Think of a course or a tutorial on a technical tool. Write one moment that took your motivation away, one per note.


 

11:11, 5 minutes. When the countdown ends, type in the second window: /board-synthesis motivation. It takes about a minute; fill it with one moment of my own (a course where the setup failed and the instructor went on).

title: Git for Scientists
text:
What you wrote, sorted
Your moments, sorted under unpredictability, unfairness and indifference. I switch to the second tab.

For your own teaching: which of the three do your learners meet most often?


11:16, 4 minutes. Switch to live.html, second slide. Read two notes per heading. Ask for one hand per heading. If the synthesis failed: read six notes from the board and ask the room to name the heading.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Also on my list

Peer instruction. People explain to each other and review each other’s work. It is the 30 minutes of pull requests in pairs that you did not do today.
A place for questions, and the plain statement that a short workshop does not answer all of them.
Online: a short visit to each break-out room, while the group is small enough.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Where this comes from

Brown and Wilson (2018), Ten quick tips for teaching programming: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006023
Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, free to read: https://teachtogether.tech/
The Carpentries Instructor Training, open material and a certification: https://carpentries.github.io/instructor-training/


If you teach a technical tool, take an instructor training. It is the best use of your time, out of respect for the time your learners give you.


Block 11:20 to 11:25, this slide and the one before. My own route was the RStudio instructor certification in 2020, built by Greg Wilson on the same material; it changed how I teach novices. The Carpentries training is the open route today.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Would you teach this?
Your turn
I would like to offer a workshop for people who teach Git and GitHub: this course design, its scripts and the material, for you to run with your own groups.

Answer with a commit, the step of 10:00, this time on your own. In your repository teaching-your-username:

Open the file your-username.md and add one line:
- Teach the teachers: yes / maybe / no. What I would need:
If you like, a second line: - A moment in a course that took my motivation away:
Commit to main, then Push origin.



 

Your answer commits you to nothing. No laptop setup? Write it on a note under Parked questions.


Block 11:25 to 11:30, with the last slide. The second line is a choice: unlike a note on the board, a commit carries your name. The form of the offer is open; the answers shape it. They arrive as commits, which I can read with the tracker.

Thank you
Everything stays open after today:

The website and these slides: https://gitforsci-rdc.github.io/website/

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
About 25 minutes. Due by Thursday, 19 November 2026, and at the latest Friday, 20 November, 09:00.
You create a repository of your own, write three lines about your teaching into it, copy it to your laptop and make one commit there. On Friday you bring the file with your three lines into the shared workshop repository with a pull request. The hands-on part of the workshop builds on this step.
You need Steps 3 to 5 first: GitHub Desktop is installed and signed in, and you have accepted the invitation to the organisation gitforsci-rdc.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 1: Create the repository (in the browser)
text:
Part 1: Create the repository (in the browser)

Open https://github.com/new while signed in.
Owner: choose gitforsci-rdc, not your own account.
Repository name: teaching- followed by your GitHub username, for example teaching-octocat.
Choose Private.
Tick Add a README file.
Click Create repository.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)
text:
Part 2: Write your three lines (in the browser)

In your new repository, click Add file, then Create new file.
Name the file after your GitHub username with the ending .md, for example octocat.md.
Copy these lines into the file and fill them in:
# your-username

- Who I teach:
- With which tool:
- What blocks me:
Click Commit changes…. Write the commit message Add my teaching context and click Commit changes.

A commit is one saved state of your repository, with who, when and what. You have now made your first one.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 3: Clone the repository (GitHub Desktop)
Clone a repository once. A second click on Clone makes a second copy on your laptop, and the two get mixed up.

Open GitHub Desktop. Choose the menu File, Clone Repository…, then the tab URL.
Type gitforsci-rdc/teaching- followed by your username into the first field.
Look at Local Path. It must end in gitrepos/teaching- followed by your username, in the folder gitrepos you created in Step 5.
Click Clone. GitHub Desktop shows your repository at the top left.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 4: An editor (recommended)
GitHub Desktop shows changes, but it does not edit files. I recommend Sublime Text, a free editor for plain text.

Install Sublime Text.
In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), tab Integrations, and choose Sublime Text as External Editor.

Without Sublime Text, use TextEdit on macOS or Notepad on Windows. Do not use Word.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Part 5: One commit from your laptop
text:
Part 5: One commit from your laptop

Open the file README.md of your repository. With Sublime Text: menu Repository, Open in Sublime Text, then click README.md. Without it: menu Repository, Show in Finder (Windows: Show in Explorer), then open README.md with TextEdit or Notepad.
Add one sentence below the title, for example what this repository is for. Save the file.
Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists README.md with a tick.
Write a commit message in the field at the bottom left, for example Describe this repository.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin at the top. Your commit is now on GitHub as well.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Part 6: Check and report

In GitHub Desktop, click the tab History. You see three commits: the first one made by GitHub, your three lines, and the sentence in the README.
Open your issue in the workshop repository, the one with your username in its title, and tick the box for Step 6.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Stuck?

The owner gitforsci-rdc is not in the list. The invitation is not accepted yet. Open https://github.com/orgs/gitforsci-rdc/invitation while signed in.
The push is rejected. You ticked “Block command line pushes that expose my email” in Step 4, and GitHub Desktop still uses your real address. Open Settings (Windows: File, Options), tab Git, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com and save. Then click Undo at the bottom of the tab Changes and commit again.
Something went very wrong with the clone. Delete the folder on your laptop and clone again. The version on GitHub is the latest one, as far as you pushed.
Anything else: write what you see as a comment in your issue, with a screenshot.

If this step is not finished by Friday, come anyway. You sit with a neighbour who has it, follow on their laptop and take the reviewer’s part. The educator part of the workshop needs no setup.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
About 2 minutes. Due by Thursday, 19 November 2026, and at the latest Friday, 20 November, 09:00.
Every commit carries an email address. That is part of Git and no problem in itself, but you should know which address it is. In Step 3 you chose the address for commits made on your laptop. Commits made in the browser on github.com do not follow that choice. They carry the address you sign in with, unless you change one account setting.
The workshop repository stays private to the course organisation. The setting matters for every repository of yours that is or becomes public.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Steps
If you want your email address to stay out of your commits:

Open https://github.com/settings/emails.
Tick Keep my email addresses private.
Tick Block command line pushes that expose my email.

The setting applies to all new commits.
Next: Step 5.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
To set up an account on GitHub, follow these general steps:

Go to the GitHub website at https://github.com/.
Click on the “Sign up” button on the top right corner of the page.
Enter your preferred username, email address, and password in the provided fields.
Choose whether you want to receive updates and announcements via email.
Complete the verification process by solving a puzzle and entering a verification code sent to your email.







TipUsername advice from: Happy Git and GitHub for the useR





You will be able to upgrade to a paid level of service, apply discounts, join organizations, etc. in the future, so don’t fret about any of that now. Except your username. You might want to give that some thought.
A few tips, which sadly tend to contradict each other:

Incorporate your actual name! People like to know who they’re dealing with. Also makes your username easier for people to guess or remember.
Reuse your username from other contexts, e.g., Twitter or Slack. But, of course, someone with no GitHub activity will probably be squatting on that.
Pick a username you will be comfortable revealing to your future boss.
Shorter is better than longer.
Be as unique as possible in as few characters as possible. In some settings GitHub auto-completes or suggests usernames.
Make it timeless. Don’t highlight your current university, employer, or place of residence, e.g. JennyFromTheBlock.
Avoid words laden with special meaning in programming.
Avoid the use of upper vs. lower case to separate words. We highly recommend all lowercase. GitHub treats usernames in a case insensitive way, but using all lowercase is kinder to people doing downstream regular expression work with usernames, in various languages. A better strategy for word separation is to use a hyphen -.

You can change your username later, but better to get this right the first time.

https://help.github.com/articles/changing-your-github-username/
https://help.github.com/articles/what-happens-when-i-change-my-username/




Once you have created your GitHub account, enter the username in the pre-course survey if you have not done so yet, or send it to me by email: lschoebitz@ethz.ch. I then invite you to the GitHub organisation for the course.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Thank you for joining this workshop at the Research Data Conference 2026. Your instructor Lars Schöbitz, Global Health Engineering, ETH Zurich, is looking forward to meeting you.
We meet on Friday, 20 November 2026, 09:30 to 11:30 (Europe/Zurich) in Room Wytsicht, Gurten, Bern, at the Research Data Conference 2026. Conference programme and venue: https://researchdatasupport.ch/srdsn-conference. Registration runs through the conference.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Background
Git and GitHub are the connective tissue of reproducible, collaborative research, yet many researchers learn them through fragmented tutorials that stop short of the collaboration patterns that matter: branching, pull requests, review and merging. This workshop is delivered as if every participant were a learner, and the real audience is educators: data stewards, research software engineers and instructors who teach, or want to teach, similar material. You first experience a condensed version of the full course from the learner’s seat, then switch to an educator lens to judge whether you could teach it in your own context. The course is published as an open educational resource.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Prior knowledge
No experience with Git or GitHub is assumed, and no programming. The hands-on part runs in GitHub Desktop, which works for files of any kind. In the pre-course survey some of you said you work in R, some in Python and some do not programme. If you already use Git with another tool, bring that tool.

text:
What do I need to bring to the workshop?

a laptop with GitHub Desktop installed and its charger, connected to the conference wifi
a web browser (preferably Chrome or Firefox)
a pen and paper (we will be doing some drawings)
the pre-work below completed

Prior to the workshop, there is some pre-work for you to do. It keeps our two hours for the collaboration skills instead of setting up infrastructure.

What do I need to prepare before the workshop?

Step 1: Complete the pre-course survey by Monday, 16 November 2026, 18:00.
Step 2: Get an account for GitHub, if you have none.
Step 3: Install GitHub Desktop and sign in.
Step 4: Decide where your email address shows.
Step 5: Do the setup check.
Step 6: Create your own repository and make your first commit.

Steps 3 to 6 take about 60 minutes and are due by Thursday, 19 November 2026, and at the latest Friday, 20 November, 09:00. The hands-on part builds on the pre-work. Anyone who arrives without it sits with a prepared neighbour, follows on their laptop and takes the reviewer’s part, and takes full part in the educator part of the workshop.

title: Pre-course work: Git for Scientists at RDC 2026
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Collaboration patterns: make a commit in a repository of their own and follow the path of a change through branch, pull request, review and merge.
Instructional design: evaluate the workshop’s design (sequencing, scaffolding, exercises) from an educator’s perspective.
Reuse: assess whether they could reuse and adapt the material to teach Git and GitHub in their own setting.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Steps

macOSWindows



Open https://desktop.github.com/ and click Download for macOS.
Open the downloaded ZIP file in your Downloads folder. Drag the program GitHub Desktop onto the Applications folder in the sidebar of the Finder.
Start GitHub Desktop. If macOS asks whether you want to open a program from the internet, click Open.
Click Sign in to GitHub.com. Your browser opens. Sign in with your GitHub account and click Authorize desktop. Allow the browser to open GitHub Desktop.
Back in GitHub Desktop you see Configure Git. Your name and email address go into every commit you make on the laptop. Under Email, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com if you do not want to show one. GitHub still links your commits to your account. Click Finish.

You are done when the menu GitHub Desktop, Settings, tab Accounts shows your GitHub username.


GitHub Desktop installs into your user folder and as a rule needs no administrator rights. If your laptop is managed and blocks the installation, ask your IT for “GitHub Desktop” and write to me so that I know.

Open https://desktop.github.com/ and click Download for Windows (64bit).
Start the downloaded file GitHubDesktopSetup-x64.exe. The installation runs without questions and opens the program at the end.
Click Sign in to GitHub.com. Your browser opens. Sign in with your GitHub account and click Authorize desktop. Allow the browser to open GitHub Desktop.
Back in GitHub Desktop you see Configure Git. Your name and email address go into every commit you make on the laptop. Under Email, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com if you do not want to show one. GitHub still links your commits to your account. Click Finish.

You are done when the menu File, Options, tab Accounts shows your GitHub username.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Stuck?

The browser does not return to the program. Close GitHub Desktop, start it again and repeat the sign-in.
You chose the wrong address under Configure Git. Open Settings (macOS) or Options (Windows), tab Git, and change it there.
Windows warns about an unknown app. Click More info, then Run anyway. The file comes from GitHub.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
section: Before you start: one folder for all repositories
text:
Before you start: one folder for all repositories
Create a folder named gitrepos in your Documents folder. Do not put it into a folder that syncs with iCloud, OneDrive or Dropbox. Git and the sync get in each other’s way, and changes are lost.

title: Git for Scientists (RDC 2026)
text:
Steps

Accept the invitation. After you have given your GitHub username in the survey, GitHub sends you an email with the button Join @gitforsci-rdc. Or open https://github.com/orgs/gitforsci-rdc/invitation while signed in.
Open GitHub Desktop. Choose the menu File, Clone Repository…, then the tab URL.
Type gitforsci-rdc/workshop into the first field.
Look at Local Path before you click anything else. Click Choose…, go to Documents, select gitrepos and confirm. The path must end in gitrepos/workshop.
Click Clone. GitHub Desktop shows Current Repository: workshop at the top left.
Open the issues of the workshop repository and click the one with your username in its title. Tick the boxes and write the comment setup complete.

You are done when your comment stands in your issue.

text:
Stuck?

No invitation. I can only invite you once I have your username. Complete the survey and look again an hour later.
GitHub Desktop says the repository was not found. The invitation is not accepted yet, or GitHub Desktop is signed in with a different account. Check Settings or Options, tab Accounts.
The path ends in a folder named Untitled (macOS). Click Choose… again and select gitrepos without typing a name.
Anything else: write what you see as a comment in your issue, with a screenshot.

Next: Step 6.
If the setup is not finished by Friday, come anyway. You sit with a neighbour who has it, follow on their laptop and take the reviewer’s part. The educator part of the workshop needs no setup.

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
In the workshop you watched a file go into the shared repository. This page has the same steps for you, to do at home. You bring the file with your three lines into the shared repository workshop, on a branch of your own and through a pull request. Lars reads it, asks one question and merges it.
Open your pull request by Friday 4 December 2026. Lars reviews the pull requests that are open by that date.
Steps 1 to 5 open the pull request. Step 6 is the review: a question from Lars, your answer as a commit, and the merge.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Before you start
You need the finished pre-work:

the repository workshop, cloned in Step 5 to Documents/gitrepos/workshop
your own repository teaching-your-username with the file your-username.md, cloned in Step 6 to Documents/gitrepos/teaching-your-username

Is something missing? Go through Step 5 and Step 6 of the pre-work first.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 1: open the shared repository
You cloned workshop in Step 5. Do not clone it again.

Open GitHub Desktop. Click Current Repository at the top left and choose workshop.
Click Fetch origin at the top. If the button then reads Pull origin, click it once more. Your copy now has the latest state of main.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 2: create a branch
A branch is a line of work of your own in the shared repository. You can add files on it without touching main.

Click Current Branch at the top, then New Branch.
As the name, write people- followed by your GitHub username, for example people-octocat. Click Create Branch.
The top now reads Current Branch: people-your-username.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 3: copy your file
You copy the one file with your three lines from your own repository into the shared one. Your own repository stays as it is.
Copy the file, never the whole folder teaching-your-username. The folder carries a hidden folder named .git, and Git would then see a repository inside a repository.

macOSWindows



In Finder, open Documents/gitrepos/teaching-your-username.
Click the file your-username.md once and press Command and C.
Open Documents/gitrepos/workshop/people and press Command and V.




In Explorer, open Documents\gitrepos\teaching-your-username.
Click the file your-username.md once and press Ctrl and C.
Open Documents\gitrepos\workshop\people and press Ctrl and V.




The folder people now holds _example.md and your file.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 4: commit

Go back to GitHub Desktop. The tab Changes lists people/your-username.md with a tick.
Write a message in the field Summary at the bottom left, for example Add my teaching context.
The button below now reads Commit 1 file to people-your-username. If it ends in to main, you are on the wrong branch. Go back to step 2.
Click the button.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
section: Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
text:
Step 5: publish the branch and open the pull request
Your branch exists only on your laptop so far.

Click Publish branch at the top. GitHub Desktop pushes the branch with your commit to GitHub.
Click the blue button Preview Pull Request. A window shows your file.
At the top it reads base: main and compare: people-your-username. That is how it should be. Click Create Pull Request at the bottom right. Your browser opens on github.com.
The text field holds a template with two lines. Fill in File with people/your-username.md.
On the right, click Reviewers and type larnsce. Choose the name from the list.
Click the green button Create pull request.

Your pull request is open. Do not merge it yourself, also when GitHub shows you the button. Reading by a second person is the point of the exercise.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Step 6: review, answer, merge
You are the author of the pull request, Lars is the reviewer.

Lars: writes one question on a line of your file. GitHub sends you a notification by email.
You: open your pull request in the list of pull requests. You see the comment there. Answer it in the file: open Documents/gitrepos/workshop/people/your-username.md in your editor, change the line and save. In GitHub Desktop, write a commit message, click Commit 1 file to people-your-username, then Push origin. The open pull request shows the new commit. You need no second pull request.
Lars: reads your commit and merges the pull request.
You: in GitHub Desktop, click Current Branch and choose main. Click Fetch origin, then Pull origin. The folder people on your laptop now holds the files of everyone who is merged.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Done when
Your pull request stands under closed pull requests with the purple mark Merged, and your file is in the folder people on main.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Add your file with a pull request
text:
Stuck?

A commit on main instead of your branch. As long as you have not pushed, GitHub Desktop shows the button Undo at the bottom left, below the commit. Click it. Then create the branch (step 2). GitHub Desktop asks whether your changes should come along. Choose to bring them to the new branch.
Nothing appears in the tab Changes. The file is in a different place. It belongs into gitrepos/workshop/people.
Changes shows a folder instead of one file. You copied the repository folder. Delete the copied folder from workshop/people and copy only the file your-username.md.
The push is rejected. Your commit carries your real email address, and your account blocks such pushes. In GitHub Desktop, open Settings (Windows: File, Options), Git, tab Author, choose the address that ends in @users.noreply.github.com and click Save. Then click Undo at the bottom of the tab Changes and commit again.
Publish branch is missing, the top reads Push origin. The branch is published already. Click Push origin if commits are missing and go on with step 5.
The name is not in the list of reviewers. Go on without a reviewer. Lars sees every new pull request in the repository.
Anything else: write a comment in your issue in the workshop repository.
crumbs: Add your file with a pull request

title: Git for Scientists
text:
On your feet: Danish clapping
Our turn With your neighbour, standing, face to face.


Slap your thighs with both hands.
Both hands to the left, to the right or up. You choose, your neighbour chooses.
Slap your thighs again.
Did you both choose the same? Clap each other’s hands. If not, choose again.



Three rounds, each one faster than the one before.


Block 10:40 to 10:45. Show it with one volunteer first, slowly, and count out loud. Three rounds of under a minute. Whoever prefers to sit does it seated or watches. Then: sit down, open the board.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Feedback you ask for yourself
You choose the questions, the room answers in writing, and nobody has to speak. Examples from a cooking class:









Positive
Negative




Content
The reason for resting the dough was new to me
Three terms came without an explanation


Presentation
I could see the hands from the back row
The recipe on the screen was too small to read


Interaction
We tasted each other’s results
Questions were only taken at the end




One point per note. A point I can act on names what happened, as these do.


Rubric: Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together, slides on feedback, CC BY 4.0


Block 10:45 to 10:55, together with the next slide. Asking for feedback yourself, with your own questions, is the first advice in the book. Read two cells out loud, one positive and one negative. The examples are from a cooking class so that I put no words about this morning into your heads.

title: Git for Scientists
text:
Five things I do

Words I leave out: just easily quickly. A learner who is stuck on the step hears: it is me.
Design for the novice: every click is written down, and extra material is marked as extra.
Know the learners, then design: 27 survey answers decided the software and the pairs. The content of today was written yesterday.
A learner account: every demo ran as rainbow-train, with the rights you have, on the screens you see.
Type with the room, mistakes included: I type, you type, nothing is pasted.


Each point has a slide of its own at the end of this deck.


Block 11:10 to 11:15. One sentence per point, each with its example from this morning. Found one of the three words on my slides or in the pre-work? Park it on the board, I fix it in a commit after the workshop.
